newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher, yields at 3-month lows.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher, yields at 3-month lows.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended higher on Friday and yields fell to three-month lows after buyers erased early losses incurred after the government reported that U.S. unemployment fell to a 23-year low in May.

The government offered a mixed picture of the U.S. labor market, reporting that the U.S. unemployment rate had fallen to 4.8 percent, its lowest level in 23 years, but also reporting a sharp deceleration in job growth for the month.
Payrolls expanded by 138,000 jobs in May after swelling by 323,000 new jobs in April.
Economists had anticipated job growth of 219,000 jobs in May and a 5.0 pct unemployment rate.

The data are important to the U.S. credit markets because investors and monetary policy makers worry that tight job markets will encourage workers to demand big pay hikes, a trend that could fan the embers of inflation.
Payroll growth has averaged 229,000 new jobs a month since the start of the year and in May, average hourly earnings rose four cents an hour to $12.19.
Economists said the May employment report supported the notion that the economy was strong.
And Joseph Dziwura, economist at The Sakura Bank, said May's modest jobs growth could mean June would see a more vigorous payroll expansion.

Government securities prices see-sawed immediately after the employment report. Prices fell, recovered, and fell again as analysts debated whether the May labor market data nudged the Federal Reserve closer to another interest-rate hike.
Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Bank of Montreal, said that what the Fed would do at its next policy meeting on July 1-2 was still open to wide debate.

The slowing in May employment growth could bolster Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's confidence "that the economy, in general, and consumer spending, in particular, will slow to a sustainable pace in coming quarters," O'Neill said.

In late morning trade, however, U.S. Treasury prices turned higher. Talk of a delay in the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was said to spur foreign buying of U.S. assets. Retail accounts jumped in. Traders spoke of Asian central bank purchases of two-year notes and there was rumored buying by a Middle East account.
Technical buying emerged as the September T-bond futures contract overcame technical resistance at 110-10/32.
As prices moved higher, traders who had set up short positions based on the view that prices would fall were forced to purchase securities to cover their short positions.
The Federal Reserve's mid-afternoon report that consumer installment credit had expanded by $7.6 billion in April from a revised $3.1 billion in March had scant impact.
The market finished at session highs.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-1/32, up 1-8/32, its yield having fallen to 6.78 percent, the lowest closing yield since February 26.

Two-year notes ended at 100-9/32, up 6/32 to yield 6.10 percent. Five-year notes rose 14/32 to 100-16/32 to yield 6.38 percent and the 10-year note was up 28/32 to 100-30/32, its yield at 6.50 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell five basis points to 4.92 percent, six-month rates fell three basis points to 5.37 percent and year bill rates dropped six basis points to 5.38 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
Bill rates continued to perform the best on the yield curve, but dealers said the low supply of bills was keeping rates low.

The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down eight basis points points at 4.82 percent. The six-month bill rate fell two basis points to 5.19 percent. The year bill rate was down six basis points at 5.46 percent.
The five-year note traded up 13/32 at 99-31/32 to yield 6.52 percent. The 10-year note closed up 18/32 at 99-23/32, yielding 6.67 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
